title: In-group Bias (Minimal Group Paradigm)
description: People automatically favor those they perceive as belonging to their own group—even when the group is completely random or meaningless. The bias kicks in instantly, often without awareness.
shortDescription: People automatically favor those they perceive as belonging to their own group—even when the group is completely random or meaningless. The bias kicks in instantly, often without awareness.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: People automatically favor those they perceive as belonging to their own group—even when the group is completely random or meaningless. The bias kicks in instantly, often without awareness.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A sports fan celebrates a win by “their” team as if they personally contributed.
In an office, people from the same university help each other more, even if they didn’t know each other before.
A study showed that when people were randomly assigned to “red team” or “blue team” based on a coin toss, they immediately rated their own team members as more likeable and gave them more rewards.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Using “we” and “us” for an arbitrary group.
Viewing the out‑group as less competent, less trustworthy, or less deserving.
Sharing resources generously with in‑group members, stingily with out‑group.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel a flash of preference for someone just because you share a trivial trait (birthday, hometown, sports team).
The group you’re in suddenly feels superior, and you didn’t notice that happening.
Decisions about hiring, promotions, or friendships are swayed by “fit” that is really “similarity.”

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Henri Tajfel (1971) showed that even minimal, meaningless groups create bias. We categorize the world to simplify it, and we attach our self‑esteem to our groups. Favoring the in‑group boosts our own self‑worth.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When evaluating someone, ask: “Would my judgment change if they were in my group?”
Create cross‑cutting categories: mix teams, remind people of shared superordinate goals.
Be aware that “cultural fit” can be a cover for in‑group bias.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you don’t have biases because you’re open‑minded. In‑group bias operates beneath conscious awareness.
Assuming you can eliminate it entirely. You can’t, but you can manage its effects.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A hiring committee interviews two equally qualified candidates. One went to the same college as the CEO. The CEO says, “I just felt a connection.” The candidate is hired. The other, from a lesser‑known school but with a slightly better record, is passed over. The CEO never saw his own bias.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: A “connection” is often just recognition. Your brain mistakes “familiar” for “superior” in a split second.
